faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other such that, from Earth's perspective, one star periodically passes in front of the other. Each time this happens, the total brightness we receive from the system dips noticeably. By observing these brightness dips - called eclipses - we can measure the orbital period (how long one complete orbit takes) and compare the depths of successive eclipses to learn about the stars' sizes and orbital geometry.
faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary star?

faqs.answer: A candidate is any eclipsing binary signal that passes Star Vetter's initial statistical checks and does not match any known object in our reference catalogs. A confirmed result is a candidate that has also passed an automated pixel-level check - a technical examination that ensures the eclipse signal originates from the target star and not from a nearby background star whose light is blending into the measurement. All 120 results listed on this site are confirmed in that specific sense.
faqs.question: What's the difference between a 'candidate' and a 'confirmed' result here?

faqs.answer: Star Vetter uses a machine learning model (histogram gradient boosting, trained on 1,183 labeled examples) as a second opinion on candidate quality. This model outperforms the rule-based baseline that currently decides which candidates undergo pixel-level checking. However, the ML score itself is not used to filter or gate which candidates are checked - it is a comparison tool and research output only, showing that machine learning can refine the vetting process beyond hand-crafted rules.
faqs.question: What is the machine learning score?

faqs.answer: Each candidate undergoes an automated pixel-level check that examines the spatial distribution of the eclipse signal across the detector pixels. This check confirms whether the brightness dip originates from the target star or from a nearby object whose light contaminates the measurement. This is a fully automated computational process, not a manual inspection. Candidates that pass this check are confirmed and listed on the site.
faqs.question: How does Star Vetter check that a candidate is real?

faqs.answer: Star Vetter uses an odd/even eclipse-depth test: it compares the brightness depth of odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered eclipses. If these depths differ significantly, it suggests the measured period may be an alias (a harmonic or fraction of the true period), and such candidates are flagged with this caveat. Users should check the individual candidate page to see if this flag applies.
faqs.question: What happens if the eclipse pattern looks like it could repeat at two different periods?

faqs.answer: Yes. Each confirmed candidate includes a light curve plot and measured orbital period and eclipse depths. If you have access to TESS data or other photometric surveys, you can download the light curve and examine the eclipses yourself. The information provided should allow independent assessment of the signal quality and eclipse properties.
faqs.question: Can I verify a result myself?

faqs.answer: Being listed on Star Vetter represents the end of the automated pipeline's work. The site itself does not conduct follow-up observations, add candidates to official star catalogs, or guide other researchers' work. The results are made public here as a resource; what happens next - whether other astronomers choose to observe, characterize, or study these systems further - is beyond the scope of this project.
faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it appears on this site?

faqs.answer: Star Vetter has sampled and attempted to obtain light curves for 7,880 TESS targets. This represents roughly 0.9 percent of the ~872,000 targets TESS can observe. The full survey is ongoing, and coverage will grow over time as more TESS data becomes available.
faqs.question: How much of the sky has Star Vetter examined?

narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies candidate eclipsing binary stars in data from NASA's TESS satellite. When two stars orbit each other and pass in front of one another from our viewpoint, their combined brightness dips in a characteristic pattern. Star Vetter searches TESS light curves for these patterns, then vets each candidate through multiple checks: statistical quality gates, cross-matching against six major variable-star catalogs to avoid re-identifying known objects, and an automated pixel-level check to confirm the signal comes from the target star itself rather than a nearby contaminant. So far, the pipeline has confirmed 120 candidates from a sample of nearly 7,900 targets. Each confirmed candidate is listed here with its light curve and measured orbital period and eclipse depths. These results are trustworthy because they survive a rigorous, multi-stage funnel designed to catch instrumental artifacts and false positives before confirmation.
